blocks.text: Isaiah 56:1-8 presents communal restoration as inseparable from justice, Sabbath-keeping, and the welcome of foreigners and eunuchs who hold fast to the covenant. The chapter’s promise of a house of prayer for all peoples therefore belongs with its insistence that the community’s life be marked by justice rather than exclusion.

Isaiah 56 stands at the beginning of the book’s final major division, Isaiah 56-66. The received book is widely studied as a long-collected and edited work spanning several historical horizons, although no detailed reconstruction has won consensus. That makes this division a useful reading map, not proof of a simple author-by-author scheme.

Isaiah’s welcome of faithful foreigners is important when reading biblical passages that address membership and access. Nehemiah 13 applies an exclusion concerning Ammonites and Moabites in the setting of Tobiah’s access to temple space; alongside that episode, Ruth and texts such as Isaiah 56 caution against treating the passage as a universal ethnic ban.

Isaiah 56:7 is later taken up in the account of Jesus’ temple action in Mark. One disputed reading understands Mark’s fig-tree scene and temple action together as an interpretation of Jerusalem’s leadership and the temple in relation to fruit, prayer, the nations, commerce, and judgment. That reading must not be used to justify contempt for Judaism or for sacred places.
